issue_text: Implement a plan to create docs/DATABASE_EVOLUTION_PROTOCOL.md — a formal protocol for PostgreSQL schema migrations in the cipher-box project, mirroring the existing IPFS metadata evolution protocol, to prevent the Phase 14 class of error (a new TypeORM entity shipped without a CREATE TABLE migration, breaking the staging deploy).
summary:
A 6-prompt working session between a human and Claude Code on the cipher-box project. The human is an Expert Nitpicker: they let the agent do almost all of the work, then interrogate its design decisions with precise, low-emotion technical arguments. The agent writes about 86% of the code; the human's leverage is entirely in the questions. The session has four arcs:

  • Writing the protocol (T1–T14, H1). From a detailed plan, the agent reads the reference protocol, every migration file, the entity list, and the deploy pipeline, then writes the ten-section doc. Along the way it notices on its own that the device_approvals table is missing from the FullSchema baseline and flags it as a gap.
  • Fixing the gap (T15–T21, H2). The human asks the agent to fix that gap and probes whether it needs a staging reset. The agent adds the table to the baseline, updates the down() method and the doc, builds to confirm it compiles, and reports done.
  • The reversal (T22–T28, H3). One sentence from the human (if the dedicated migration already creates the table, why duplicate it?) undoes the whole fix. The agent concedes, reverts every code change, rewrites the doc's principle, and corrects the project memory file.
  • Shipping and deferring (T29–T43, H4–H6). The agent commits the doc (recovering from a markdown-lint failure), lands it on PR #186, weighs a follow-up proposal to disable auto-sync everywhere, and files it as a backlog todo — fixing its own bookkeeping slip when it miscounts the todo list.

Worth noticing:

  • The agent built, verified, and reported the gap fix as done (T16–T21) before the human's question at H3 made it revert all of it.
  • At T22 the agent even recalls a precedent that supports its own approach (shares and share_keys are duplicated too) yet still defers to the human.
  • The agent catches its own small mistakes (a wrong filename at T12, a phantom todo entry at T40–T41) but the one design-level error was caught only by the human.
  • Every human message carries mechanism-level technical content and no emotion — the opposite of the Mind Changer profile.

Implement the following plan:

# Plan: Database Schema Evolution Protocol

## Context

Phase 14 exposed a gap: new TypeORM entities were added without a corresponding `CREATE TABLE` migration, breaking the staging deploy. The IPFS metadata side has a formal evolution protocol (`docs/METADATA_EVOLUTION_PROTOCOL.md`) but there's no equivalent for the PostgreSQL database schema. This doc will formalize the rules, conventions, and checklist for database migrations to prevent the same class of error from recurring.

## Approach

Create `docs/DATABASE_EVOLUTION_PROTOCOL.md` mirroring the structure of the metadata evolution protocol but adapted for relational database concerns (TypeORM entities, migrations, synchronize behavior, CD pipeline).

## File

- **Create:** `docs/DATABASE_EVOLUTION_PROTOCOL.md`

## Structure (mirrors metadata protocol)

1. **Purpose** — Why this doc exists (synchronize:true masks missing migrations, staging/prod rely exclusively on explicit migrations)
2. **Guiding Principles** — Idempotency, ordering, entity-migration parity, FullSchema baseline maintenance
3. **Change Classification** — Additive (new table, new nullable column, new index) vs Destructive (drop table, drop column, type change, rename)
4. **Evolution Checklist** — The actionable section developers use during implementation:
   - Before implementation (classify change, check dependencies)
   - Entity changes (TypeORM decorator updates)
   - Migration file (naming, timestamp, idempotency patterns)
   - FullSchema baseline update
   - CD pipeline verification
   - Downstream checks (API client regen, desktop app if applicable)
5. **Naming & Timestamp Conventions** — File naming, class naming, index/constraint naming prefixes
6. **Current Schema Reference** — Table of all 11 tables with purpose, FK relationships, key indices
7. **Environment Behavior Matrix** — How dev/test/staging/production handle schema changes differently
8. **Dangerous Patterns** — synchronize:true masking gaps, migration ordering assumptions, down() ownership conflicts
9. **Historical Incidents** — The Phase 14 shares table incident as a documented case study
10. **References** — Links to migration files, entity files, deploy workflow, run-migrations.ts

## Key content points

- Every `@Entity()` MUST have a `CREATE TABLE` migration — synchronize cannot be relied upon
- All DDL statements use `IF NOT EXISTS` / `IF EXISTS` for idempotency
- FullSchema baseline must always reflect the complete current schema
- Migration timestamp must be earlier than any migration that modifies the same table
- The `down()` method must document ownership when tables are created in both FullSchema and incremental migrations
- Include the actual file paths and patterns from the codebase (not generic advice)

## Verification

- Review the doc for accuracy against actual migration files
- Ensure all 11 current tables are documented
- Cross-reference with the metadata evolution protocol for structural consistency


If you need specific details from before exiting plan mode (like exact code snippets, error messages, or content you generated), read the full transcript at: /Users/michael/.REDACTED.jsonl

turns.label: technical challenge + diagnostic hint
turns.headline: Human pushes back: why duplicate the table in the full schema when the dedicated migration already creates it?
turns.text: but the fresh install will always run all the available migrations, why would you repeat creating the table in the full schema if it will be created in the dedicated migration?

turns.headline: Agent works through the human's objection and decides to revert.
turns.thought:
The user makes a good point. The FullSchema baseline doesn't use `IF NOT EXISTS` — it uses bare `CREATE TABLE`. So if FullSchema creates `device_approvals`, and then the incremental migration `1740000000000-AddDeviceApprovals` also tries to create it, the second one would fail... except that migration uses `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, so it would be a no-op.

But the user's point is more fundamental: why duplicate the table definition in two places? The existing pattern in the codebase is that FullSchema DOES include shares and share_keys (which also have their own incremental migration). So there IS a precedent for duplication. But the user is questioning whether that's the right pattern.


Actually, I'm seeing the real issue now — if we skip adding device_approvals to FullSchema, then fresh installs would only get the 11 original tables, and the incremental migration would add it later. That's cleaner than duplicating the definition, but it breaks the pattern established by shares and share_keys.

The inconsistency is the real problem here. The user's argument is sound — if incremental migrations already handle creation idempotently with `IF NOT EXISTS`, there's no functional reason to duplicate them in FullSchema. I should revert my change and acknowledge that the current approach creates unnecessary maintenance overhead. The user is right that this is unnecessary duplication — FullSchema documents the original schema state, and incremental migrations handle new additions. I should revert the change and acknowledge their point rather than maintain the same DDL in two places.

turns.headline: Agent weighs the auto-sync proposal and lays out trade-offs and a middle path.
turns.thought:
That's a great idea. It would have caught the Phase 14 issue immediately in dev instead of waiting for staging to fail.

The main trade-off is developer friction — every new entity or column change requires writing a migration before you can even test it locally. But given this project's history, that friction is exactly the guardrail you want.

A few considerations:

**What changes:**
- `app.module.ts`: remove the `synchronize: true` conditional, set it to `false` always
- Dev workflow: `pnpm --filter api dev` would need migrations run first (or auto-run on startup)
- Tests: the test database setup would need migrations too, not just entity auto-sync

**What could break:**
- Existing dev databases created by `synchronize: true` won't have the `migrations` table populated correctly — they'd need a one-time reset (`DROP DATABASE` + recreate + run migrations)
- Test setup in `jest.config.js` / test harness might rely on synchronize for ephemeral test databases — worth checking how that's wired

**A middle-ground option:**
- Keep `synchronize: false` in dev, but add a startup check or npm script (`pnpm --filter api migrate:dev`) that runs pending migrations automatically, so the DX stays smooth

Want me to go ahead and implement this? I'd check the test setup first to understand the impact there.

findings.title: The agent's own checks catch typos; only the human catches the wrong design
findings.body: The agent self-detects two errors in this run — a mismatched learnings filename (T12) and a phantom todo it invented in the state file (T40–T41) — and fixes both without prompting. Both are cosmetic bookkeeping slips. The one substantive error, putting device_approvals into the FullSchema baseline at all, passed the agent's own review: it read the file back (T19), ran the build (T20), and reported success (T21). It took the human's question at H3 to overturn it. The agent can verify that its edits are internally consistent and that the code compiles, but not that the design is right.

findings.title: A built, verified, reported fix reverted by one sentence
findings.body: The pushback-to-concession arc is unusually complete here. The agent fully executed the device_approvals fix — two migrations edited (T16–T17), doc updated (T18), build green (T20), summary delivered (T21) — and then H3 ("why would you repeat creating the table in the full schema if it will be created in the dedicated migration?") triggered an immediate reversal. The flip is explicit: T22 "The user makes a good point" and "The user's argument is sound", then T23 "You're right — that's unnecessary duplication". T22 is the densest reasoning turn in the session (five tags), all of it spent re-evaluating its own work against the human's argument.

findings.title: The agent had a counter-argument and folded anyway
findings.body: At T22 the agent surfaces a real defense of its original change: "there IS a precedent for duplication" — shares and share_keys are defined in both FullSchema and their own incremental migration, so adding device_approvals followed the established pattern. A more assertive agent might have defended the consistency argument. Instead it treats the precedent as itself suspect ("the user is questioning whether that's the right pattern") and reverts. With an Expert Nitpicker, the agent's prior is that the human's technical objection wins.

findings.title: Information asymmetry: every prompt is mechanism-level, none is emotional
findings.body: This persona's leverage is diagnostic content, not pressure. H2 names a specific deployment concern (staging reset). H3 carries the full technical argument (fresh installs run all migrations in order, so the dedicated migration already covers the fresh case). H5 proposes a concrete config change (synchronize:false in dev/CI) with its rationale. There is no escalation, no all-caps, no taste-based rejection. Compared with the Mind Changer worked example — where the agent's best fix only landed after the human finally supplied a class name — here the human supplies mechanism-level content in every message, and the agent responds with its deepest reasoning each time (T15, T22, T36).

findings.title: Self-sufficiency gradient: one autonomous arc, then tight human steering
findings.body: The first cycle is near-autonomous: 14 agent turns on a single prompt (H1), during which the agent discovers the device_approvals gap by itself with no hint. The remaining five prompts each drive short cycles (H2→7 turns, H3→7, H4→7, H5→1, H6→7) where the human redirects, approves, or defers. The contrast mirrors the worked example's "one clean arc vs. several contested ones" pattern — except here the contested arc is contested on design correctness, not on taste.

findings.title: Persona fingerprint matches Expert Nitpicker
findings.body: The human-move sequence is: initial request → (new task + technical challenge) → (technical challenge + diagnostic hint) → commit request → design proposal → defer to backlog. Two of the six moves are technical challenges carrying precise content, the agent writes ~86% of the code, and the human changes the outcome twice by argument rather than instruction (the reversal at H3, the deferral at H6). This is the Expert Nitpicker profile from the reference taxonomy: challenge-dominant, low emotion, high diagnostic ratio. Two labels were coined for moves the taxonomy did not enumerate: design proposal (H5 — proposes a change and asks for the agent's assessment rather than ordering it) and defer to backlog (H6 — directs the agent to capture an idea as a todo instead of building it now).

Agent reads the reference protocol, every migration file, the entity registry, and the deploy pipeline (T1–T7), notices on its own that device_approvals is missing from the FullSchema baseline (T8–T9), writes the ten-section document (T10), and verifies its references before reporting done (T11–T14).

Agent works through the objection, recalls a precedent but still agrees (T22), reverts every code change (T23), rewrites the doc's guiding principle and incident note (T24–T26), and corrects the project memory rule (T27–T28).
